full_text: All right, good afternoon, and thank you for joining us this afternoon for a press conference on the EU's anti-corruption directive, which just got its final approval in Plenary about half an hour ago. This press conference is web-streamed, and we have with us today EP President Metzela. Thank you for joining us, as well as the rapporteur, Raquel García Hermida Vandervalle. We are very thankful that the president could join us, but since she has to leave fairly shortly, we will first start with her statement and then perhaps a question or two for her before she has to leave us. No, no, no, no. Don't worry. I would like to cherish as much time I have with Raquel on this podium. So thank you very much. and good afternoon to you all. I really want to start by thanking Raquel Garcia Hermida Vandervalle, the rapporteur whose first of all negotiation and drafting skills have meant that the Parliament has delivered on a key promise that we have made to people across the European Union. I'm truly grateful for the efforts of the entire negotiating team and everyone involved in the excellent work that has led to today's successful allow me also a particular mention to the shadow reporters as well. I see David Kaza here and as a compatriot from the country we know best, I know how personal the fight is for him too. Today we established the EU's first ever directive harmonising criminal laws to fight corruption. This directive is an important milestone in our fight and I'm immensely proud of the efforts made and the results achieved. For too long legislation has been fragmented, Across our union, differences between member states could be exploited, allowing corruption to persist. And with this directive, we will really close the gaps. We are establishing common standards, creating a unified definition of corruption offences and introducing minimum penalties, clear rules applied consistently across Europe. This will help our institutions, it will help our businesses, it will help our people. This is ultimately the European approach we need. It strengthens our union's resilience and effectiveness, and the message today could not be clearer that corruption has no place in our Europe, and we will keep fighting against it. So, Raquel, thank you so much for delivering something strong that this Parliament has called for. I'll take one few seconds to just have a final word on another file that was voted on today. which is the AI simplification package. We've spent a lot of time discussing the speed with which the Parliament reacts, acts on issues that are urgent. This package took us less than two months to finalise. It is another example of the European Parliament delivering with unprecedented speed on what matters most to our citizens and businesses. We understand the urgency and we're acting on it, whether it is strengthening our competitiveness, our security, or our democratic system. So I would like to congratulate Ms. Kokkalari and Mr. McNamara to have worked so well together on this. Yes, please, Madam Rapporteur. Thank you. Thank you so much, Madam President, dear Roberta. Thank you for joining us here today. Thank you to all present here. It's been quite a ride, I can say. And I'm very, very grateful that you are here representing the Parliament institutionally. But also, I would like to thank my shadow rapporteurs. David, thank you for being here today. It has really been a common effort. And I said it yesterday in my intervention in Plenary during the debate. Every major European step forward is, per definition, a collective effort. So I am very, very thankful to everyone involved. The directive we adopted today was historic. It's a binding law to tackle corruption all around the European Union, a law which closes loopholes criminals exploit and strengthens Europe's ability to prevent, detect, and prosecute corruption. With this law, Europe becomes safer as a whole. And that is important. And I would like to start by remembering and honoring people that sadly cannot celebrate with us. Slovak investigative reporter Jan Kuciak and his fiancee Martina Kuznetova. The passengers on a bus on a road that was poorly maintained near Svoga, Bulgaria. The travelers, most of them students in their 20s, on trains near Tempe, Greece, running on tracks that were out of date. Those just waiting under a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, Serbia, right outside our Union candidate country. And journalist Dafna Karuana Galicia, who exposed corruption in Malta. And without a doubt, so many more may be unknown to most of us. And all of them had hopes and dreams for their lives in Europe. But they're no longer among us as a result of corruption and fraud, sometimes at the highest level. Corruption kills. It costs us billions. It hurts trust in our governments. It undermines our democracy and eventually our union. And let me back that up with some numbers. 68% of people in the EU and 62% of companies based in the EU consider that corruption is widespread in their country. Corruption is by its nature difficult to quantify, but even conservative estimates suggest that it costs the EU our economy, our taxpayers, at least 120 billion per year. And the most far-reaching estimates bring that up close to 900 billion. Corruption, more and more intertwined with transnational international crime, does not understand borders and differences in legal provisions. And this is why I'm happy to report on key achievements secured by this Parliament. Some of them have been mentioned already by the President. I would like to highlight a couple more. Mandatory national anti-corruption strategies and a focus on prevention measures. Reinforced cooperation between national authorities and EU bodies. Annual publication of corruption data in accessible formats. And clear rules for liability of legal persons. Did this Parliament want more? Yes, yes, of course. Yes, we did. It is no secret that the negotiations with the Council were far from easy. And our work is not done and won't be done for a very long time. This directive is the beginning and will be soon complemented with a new anti-corruption strategy to be presented by the European Commission. And I trust that the European Commission will also commit to ensuring timely and appropriate implementation of the directive by the member states and acts there and when needed. And as parliaments, we will also be monitoring this process very closely. Thank you again, and I look forward to answering your questions. All right, thank you. Now we have some time for questions online or in the room. Please state your name and media. Is there anyone? Yes, and first, if we can get questions for the president before she has to leave. Is that OK? Yes, so maybe we will group two together to keep a good pace. So please, over there. And yeah, you can start. Yes, thank you. Hello, I'm President Simon Van Der Rippe for Follow the Money. I wanted to ask two questions. First is on how the European Parliament itself deals with corruption. There have been a number of cases over the past years. We've seen, for instance, in the latest Huawei affair that it is taking almost a year so far for requests to lift the immunity of MEPs for that to be handled. So, yeah, what is going on there? And secondly, the EPBO has also criticized different EU institutions, including the European Parliament, for not referring enough crime reports to the prosecutors. I believe the last published statistics for the year 2024, there were zero crime reports. Many other institutions had several crime reports. So, yes, how is the European Parliament itself dealing with corruption in its day-to-day cooperation with prosecutors? And then maybe for Raquel, a question on the... One of the things that I'm seeing in my practice as a journalist is that the main issues with corruption cases is that they tend to take ages. So what is this directive doing to reduce the duration of corruption proceedings? Thank you. Thank you very much. First of all, I will not comment on ongoing judicial investigations, and I can assure you that we cooperate fully, as I have said. done since I became president of this institution with all officials, with all institutions that require information from us. And we ourselves have internally procedures that we follow extremely carefully ever since what happened in December 2022 with Qatargate. You will note that we have put in place a long list of measures that had not been put in place before, and it is those measures that are also helping us as we go through individual processes and individual requests, most of which I trust my colleagues in the Legal Affairs Committee to handle with care. Perhaps more broadly, I have entered politics because I wanted to fight corruption. For me, this is a personal as well as institutional commitment. And that is why I wanted us to reform massively in order for us to become more accountable. And in fact, this directive that we voted on today will actually also strengthen the oversight in EU institutions and the cooperation between national authorities and EU bodies, including the anti-fraud office, the public prosecutor's office, Europol and Eurojust. Thank you. Thank you for that first answer. Thank you very much, Simon. Thank you. The first thing that every practitioner that I have met on the ground when negotiating this directive said to me is the problem is that limitation periods are way too short in many, many cases. So on the one hand, we have to prevent. On the other hand, we have to give proper legal instruments to practitioners, to prosecutors, to judges. But on the other hand, we do have to expand and extend limitation periods because we know that corruption offenses are very difficult to investigate by their own nature. And that's why I'm very happy that we have managed to extend the limitation periods in the end results to make it possible for crimes to be investigated for a long time. So I consider that one of the major wins within this directive. And I hope, I hope, and I repeat this every step of the way, that the member states won't choose for a minimalist approach, but for a maximalist approach, and they won't be joined in the lowest common denominator, but really be ambitious in the transposition of the law. The cooperation between different organizations and EU agencies is going to be important. We have made it very clear in this directive that this has to be improved and expanded. And maybe on the subject of the European institutions, I would like to make this very clear. Union officials are covered by this directive. This directive is obviously not of direct application on the institutions because it's a directive, so it's of direct application on the 27 member states, but we, as union officials, are also residents, workers, and officials of member states, and in that sense, I am also really encouraged by the text that we have taken up in the directive, in the text, that it will make it easier also for our legal system to investigate and prosecute corruption in the institutions, because I won't deny that that's, like in any government, also needed. All right. Thank you. I think we have time for one more with the president with us. So, Eddie, please, go ahead. Thank you very much, Eddie Wax, with your active. Just two questions. One on the anti-corruption directive. Isn't it ironic, Madam President, that the Parliament is calling for member states to set up independent ethics bodies when the Parliament is blocking the creation of an EU ethics body? That's the first question. On another topic, the US trade deal that was just voted today, what do you make of the votes? Because it was the parties in the centre, the socialists, EPP, Renew, that backed the deal. But the very parties that Donald Trump supports in Europe, the far right parties, you know, from what I can tell, were all against it. So does that show Donald Trump who his allies are in Europe, do you think? Thanks. So on the first point, actually, the plenary in the parliament voted in favor of the. creation of the body just before the last elections. We have already implemented comprehensive reforms and we already uphold high ethical standards. The Council is now in the lead on this and we expect the first meetings to happen soon. So we do what is expected from us and that is what we will continue to push for. On the US deal, I think the message today is that Parliament is living up to its responsibility. for bringing this deal to life. The Parliament's position in plenary on the deal received very broad support for the addition of strong safeguards, including a sunrise clause, and we act on an understanding that the 15% tariffs on most industrial goods is the ceiling, and additional tariffs will not apply above this level. We will now go directly to trialogues, and I can assure you that we want to get this across the finish line as quickly as possible in the next weeks. We see this deal as providing stability to our transatlantic partnerships and much needed, I would say, predictability. And I think that is how it was reflected in the result and the vote to our businesses on both sides of the Atlantic. And I take this opportunity to really thank the Parliament's negotiating team that brought all those concerns of our citizens together in the Parliament's position. I won't comment on who voted in favour or who voted against, but what you can see is very strong work in the centre of this House that will push the institution forward on something as important and on which the Parliament really needed to deliver. Thank you. Do you want me to leave now? Well, for us it's always nice if you can stay. I believe we still have a bit of time. I'm okay. I would like to ask something about the anti-corruption law because we know that in Italy the very crime of corruption of government agents has been abolished. And do you think that this directive can have an impact on the national legislation about this? Because the fact that this directive is seen also as you were talking of maximalist and minimalist approach. Has this directive the strength? to impose, to come back on a crime that has been abolished when it foresees that the crime is punished. Thank you. So I'll say quickly something and then Raquel, as the expert on this file, will continue. And I join her in an appeal that there will be as broad and comprehensive a transposition in all member states. perhaps by looking at the vote in the Council, Italy voted in favour of these rules, and therefore we hope that this will deliver for people in Italy and everywhere in the European Union. Thank you, Madam President Roberta, and thank you for this question. It's a very relevant one. You said, well, the offensive abuse of function has been abolished. It will have to be de-abolished. Italy will be We'll have to mandatorily criminalize at least two most serious offenses that fall in the remits of abuse of function. And I can say with all confidence that that was probably one of the most important wins in this negotiation and for this parliament. Because at some point, you really have to let our citizens show, as parliaments, that we do care about the general interests. Regardless of the political position of different member states, regardless of the political interests of different member states or governments, we stand here as Parliament for our mandate, and our mandate was very clear on the subject of abuse of function. So I'm extremely happy that Italy, even within the room provided by a directive, will have to work on this after implementation. All right, thank you. I believe that at this point we have to say goodbye to the president and continue with the rapporteur. I'm loving it here. Yeah, very sad. I'm unwanted. I get it. I get it. Thank you. Thank you very much. All right, more questions. Yes, there in the back, please. Just to follow up on this question about Italy, because it's interesting what they say from the governing... Thank you. It's interesting what they say from the governing parties of the majority. They say that what is described in Article 7 is somehow already covered by existing crimes in the Italian legislation and that this is not an introduction of a new misconduct in public office crime. So I understand from what you said you do not agree with this judgment and you see that there is the need for a new specific crime to be introduced in the legislation. I think it's not my place to get into a question of definitions with the Italian government, but if they didn't think that this was such a big deal, they wouldn't have fought against it so hard. So I guess that's the answer. All right, very succinct. And then we have towards the middle, please. Thank you. A question on the numbers. I heard you say that corruption costs the EU 120 billion a year in the most conservative estimate, up to 900 billion a year. How do you get, where do you base these numbers on and why is there such a big gap between those two estimations? Thank you so much. There are very different estimates depending on the definition of corruption that you use for the studies. These studies you can find, for example, from our own legal study service in the European Parliament, the EPRS. We can provide them to you, of course, after this press conference. And what you do see here is that if you consider fraud related to corruption as part of the sum, then you come to one estimate. If you consider corruption offenses that are penalized everywhere, only in some countries, you get to another estimate. So there is quite a big difference in the matter of definition. By the way, that is something that will also be helped by this directive, because now we know exactly what we consider to be corruption in the European Union. It is also a fact that a lot of corruption, unfortunately, goes undiscovered. So it's difficult to quantify things that are not exactly discovered, prosecuted, or judged at some point, of which we know that there are some corrupt elements being involved in the process. So that's the explanation. But again, I'm happy to provide you with the exact numbers as we get them from our specialist research service. All right. Thank you. Anyone else? And now also, if anyone online would like to raise their hand, that is also possible. All right. Going once, going twice. I think that is it for today. Then we close this press conference. Thank you all for attending. Thank you for the report, Tervins Garcia. And yeah, have a good day, everyone. Thank you for being here. Have a good day.

segments.text: Perhaps more broadly, I have entered politics because I wanted to fight corruption.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: For me, this is a personal as well as institutional commitment.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: And that is why I wanted us to reform massively in order for us to become more accountable.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: And in fact, this directive that we voted on today will actually also strengthen the oversight in EU institutions and the cooperation between national authorities and EU bodies, including

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: the anti-fraud office, the public prosecutor's office, Europol and Eurojust.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Thank you for that first answer.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Thank you very much, Simon.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: The first thing that every practitioner that I have met on the ground when negotiating this directive said to me is the problem is that limitation periods are way too short in many, many cases.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: So on the one hand, we have to prevent.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: On the other hand, we have to give

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: proper legal instruments to practitioners, to prosecutors, to judges.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: But on the other hand, we do have to expand and extend limitation periods because we know that corruption offenses are very difficult to investigate by their own nature.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: And that's why I'm very happy that we have managed to extend the limitation periods in the end results to make it possible for crimes to be investigated for a long time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: So I consider that one of the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: major wins within this directive.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: And I hope, I hope, and I repeat this every step of the way, that the member states won't choose for a minimalist approach, but for a maximalist approach, and they won't be joined in the lowest common denominator, but really be ambitious in the transposition of the law.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: The cooperation between different organizations and EU agencies is going to be important.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: We have made it very clear in this directive that this has to be improved and expanded.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: And maybe on the subject of the European institutions, I would like to make this very clear.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Union officials are covered by this directive.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: This directive is obviously not of direct application on the institutions because it's a directive, so it's of direct application on the 27 member states, but we, as union officials, are also residents, workers, and officials of member states, and in that sense,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: I am also really encouraged by the text that we have taken up in the directive, in the text, that it will make it easier also for our legal system to investigate and prosecute corruption in the institutions, because I won't deny that that's, like in any government, also needed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: I think we have time for one more with the president with us.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: So, Eddie, please, go ahead.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Thank you very much, Eddie Wax, with your active.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Just two questions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: One on the anti-corruption directive.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Isn't it ironic, Madam President, that the Parliament is calling for member states to set up independent ethics bodies when the Parliament is blocking the creation of an EU ethics body?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That's the first question.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: On another topic, the US trade deal that was just voted today, what do you make of the votes?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Because it was the parties in the centre, the socialists, EPP, Renew, that backed the deal.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: But the very parties that Donald Trump supports in Europe, the far right parties, you know, from what I can tell, were all against it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So does that show Donald Trump who his allies are in Europe, do you think?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Thanks.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: So on the first point, actually, the plenary in the parliament voted in favor of the.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: creation of the body just before the last elections.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: We have already implemented comprehensive reforms and we already uphold high ethical standards.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: The Council is now in the lead on this and we expect the first meetings to happen soon.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: So we do what is expected from us and that is what we will continue to push for.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: On the US deal, I think the message today is that Parliament is living up to its responsibility.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: for bringing this deal to life.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: The Parliament's position in plenary on the deal received very broad support for the addition of strong safeguards, including a sunrise clause, and we act on an understanding that the 15% tariffs on most industrial goods is the ceiling, and additional tariffs will not apply above this level.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: We will now go directly to trialogues, and I can assure you that we want to get this across the finish line

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: as quickly as possible in the next weeks.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: We see this deal as providing stability to our transatlantic partnerships and much needed, I would say, predictability.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: And I think that is how it was reflected in the result and the vote to our businesses on both sides of the Atlantic.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: And I take this opportunity to really thank the Parliament's negotiating team that brought all those concerns of our citizens together in the Parliament's position.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: I won't comment on who voted in favour or who voted against, but what you can see is very strong work in the centre of this House that will push the institution forward on something as important and on which the Parliament really needed to deliver.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: Do you want me to leave now?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: Well, for us it's always nice if you can stay.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: I believe we still have a bit of time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: I'm okay.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: I would like to ask something about the anti-corruption law because we know that in Italy the very crime of corruption of government agents has been abolished.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: And do you think that this directive can have an impact on the national legislation about this?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Because the fact that this directive is seen also as you were talking of maximalist and minimalist approach.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Has this directive the strength?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: to impose, to come back on a crime that has been abolished when it foresees that the crime is punished.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: So I'll say quickly something and then Raquel, as the expert on this file, will continue.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: And I join her in an appeal that there will be as broad and comprehensive a transposition in all member states.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: perhaps by looking at the vote in the Council, Italy voted in favour of these rules, and therefore we hope that this will deliver for people in Italy and everywhere in the European Union.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Thank you, Madam President Roberta, and thank you for this question.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: It's a very relevant one.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: You said, well, the offensive abuse of function has been abolished.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: It will have to be de-abolished.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Italy will be

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: We'll have to mandatorily criminalize at least two most serious offenses that fall in the remits of abuse of function.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: And I can say with all confidence that that was probably one of the most important wins in this negotiation and for this parliament.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Because at some point, you really have to let our citizens show, as parliaments, that we do care about the general interests.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Regardless of the political position of different member states, regardless of the political interests of different member states or governments, we stand here as Parliament for our mandate, and our mandate was very clear on the subject of abuse of function.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: So I'm extremely happy that Italy, even within the room provided by a directive, will have to work on this after implementation.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: All right, thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: I believe that at this point we have to say goodbye to the president and continue with the rapporteur.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: I'm loving it here.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: Yeah, very sad.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: I'm unwanted.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: I get it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: I get it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: All right, more questions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: Yes, there in the back, please.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Just to follow up on this question about Italy, because it's interesting what they say from the governing...

segments.speaker: Hablante
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: It's interesting what they say from the governing parties of the majority.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: They say that what is described in Article 7 is somehow already covered by existing crimes in the Italian legislation and that this is not an introduction of a new misconduct in public office crime.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So I understand from what you said you do not agree with this judgment and you see that there is the need for a new specific crime to be introduced in the legislation.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: I think it's not my place to get into a question of definitions with the Italian government, but if they didn't think that this was such a big deal, they wouldn't have fought against it so hard.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: So I guess that's the answer.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: All right, very succinct.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: And then we have towards the middle, please.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: A question on the numbers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: I heard you say that corruption costs the EU 120 billion a year in the most conservative estimate, up to 900 billion a year.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: How do you get, where do you base these numbers on and why is there such a big gap between those two estimations?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: There are very different estimates depending on the definition of corruption that you use for the studies.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: These studies you can find, for example, from our own legal study service in the European Parliament, the EPRS.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: We can provide them to you, of course, after this press conference.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: And what you do see here is that if you consider fraud related to corruption as part of the sum, then you come to one estimate.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: If you consider corruption offenses that are penalized everywhere, only in some countries, you get to another estimate.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: So there is quite a big difference in the matter of definition.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: By the way, that is something that will also be helped by this directive, because now we know exactly what we consider to be corruption

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: in the European Union.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: It is also a fact that a lot of corruption, unfortunately, goes undiscovered.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: So it's difficult to quantify things that are not exactly discovered, prosecuted, or judged at some point, of which we know that there are some corrupt elements being involved in the process.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: So that's the explanation.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: But again, I'm happy to provide you with the exact numbers as we get them from our specialist research service.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_07
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.text: Anyone else?
